title: Celestron AstroMaster 70AZ Refractor Telescope
tagline: A straightforward first telescope for the Moon and planets
summary: The AstroMaster 70AZ is a 70mm refractor on a simple pan-handle alt-azimuth mount and full-height tripod, with 20mm and 10mm eyepieces and a red-dot finder. Teens can explore lunar craters, Jupiter's moons and Saturn's rings, and the erect-image diagonal makes daytime nature viewing possible too.
highlights: No electronics or app needed: aim, focus and observe
Refractor design needs almost no maintenance or alignment
Works for daytime land viewing as well as the night sky
considerations: Never point it at the Sun without a proper solar filter
No age guidance from Celestron, which advises adult supervision around children

glance.bestFor: want to see Saturn's rings and Jupiter's moons
glance.inTheBox: 70mm refractor, tripod, 20mm and 10mm eyepieces, red-dot finder

title: Celestron StarSense Explorer LT 80AZ Telescope
tagline: Your phone shows exactly where to point, then you take over
summary: This 80mm refractor has a dock for a smartphone, which runs Celestron's StarSense app to recognize the star pattern overhead and list what's visible tonight. On-screen arrows guide teens as they move the manual mount until the target is centered, then they observe through 25mm and 10mm eyepieces or the included 2x Barlow.
highlights: Takes the frustration out of finding objects, a common reason beginners give up
Teens still aim the telescope by hand, so they learn the sky as they go
Larger 80mm lens gathers more light than typical entry-level scopes
considerations: Needs a compatible smartphone (Celestron lists recent iOS and Android versions)
Never point it at the Sun without a proper solar filter

glance.bestFor: want app help finding things in the night sky
glance.inTheBox: 80mm refractor, phone dock, 25mm and 10mm eyepieces, 2x Barlow

title: LEGO Technic McLaren P1 (42172)
tagline: A 1:8 hypercar with a working V8 and 7-speed gearbox
summary: This 3,893-piece Technic model builds a 1:8 scale McLaren P1 with a moving V8 piston engine, a 7-speed sequential gearbox with a shifter drum, working suspension and butterfly doors. It is a long, demanding build that shows how real drivetrains and transmissions fit together.
highlights: The gearbox and engine visibly move, which makes mechanical ideas concrete
A multi-week project for a dedicated older teen or young adult
Makes an impressive display piece once finished
considerations: LEGO rates it 18+, and its size and price suit serious builders
Takes significant shelf space once built

glance.bestFor: are dedicated builders ready for a multi-week project
glance.inTheBox: 3,893-piece 1:8 scale McLaren P1 model

title: LEGO Icons NASA Artemis Space Launch System (10341)
tagline: Build NASA's Moon rocket in 3,601 pieces
summary: This display model recreates the Artemis Space Launch System, the rocket NASA built to return astronauts to the Moon, in 3,601 pieces. It's a long, absorbing build for space fans that doubles as a talking point about modern spaceflight.
highlights: Ties directly to the current Artemis lunar program
A detailed, tall build suited to experienced builders
Great for a space-obsessed older teen or college student
considerations: LEGO rates it 18+, with a price to match
A display model with few moving functions

glance.bestFor: are space fans who love long, detailed builds
glance.inTheBox: 3,601-piece Artemis SLS rocket display model

title: Python for Kids, 2nd Edition
tagline: Learn real Python 3 by building two complete games
summary: Jason R. Briggs' book teaches Python 3 from scratch, covering variables, lists, dictionaries, loops, functions and modules, plus graphics with turtle and tkinter. Readers finish by coding two games of their own: a Pong-style game called Bounce! and a platformer called Mr. Stick Man Races for the Exit.
highlights: Uses real Python 3, the language teens will keep using in school and beyond
Ends with two complete games instead of isolated exercises
Runs on Windows, macOS, Linux or a Raspberry Pi
considerations: Needs a computer to follow along
The friendly tone may feel young to older teens

glance.bestFor: want to learn real Python by making games
glance.inTheBox: Book teaching Python 3 through two games

title: Electronics for Kids, 2nd Edition
tagline: 21 hands-on projects, from basic circuits to digital logic
summary: This fully rewritten second edition explains how electricity, resistors, capacitors, transistors and logic chips actually work, then puts each idea into a build. Across 21 projects, readers make things like an intruder alarm, an electromagnet and motor, a sunrise wake-up alarm and a secret code checker, and learn to solder along the way.
highlights: Explains why circuits behave the way they do, not just how to copy them
Moves from simple circuits all the way to digital logic
Includes a dedicated soldering chapter
considerations: Components are bought separately (the publisher offers a parts list)
Soldering projects need an iron and adult supervision

glance.bestFor: want to know why circuits work, not just copy them
glance.inTheBox: Book with 21 projects; components sold separately

title: A Beginner's Guide to Circuits
tagline: Nine quick breadboard builds with no soldering required
summary: A short, illustrated introduction to reading circuit diagrams and building on a breadboard. Readers make nine projects, including a steady-hand game, a touch-activated light, a night-light, a cookie jar alarm and a mini digital piano.
highlights: Breadboard-only projects, so there's no hot iron
Teaches how to read circuit diagrams, a skill that carries over to every later kit
A quick win for a teen who wants to try electronics first
considerations: Parts are bought separately
Pitched at beginners, so experienced teens may outgrow it quickly

glance.bestFor: want to try electronics before buying a kit
glance.inTheBox: Illustrated book with nine breadboard projects; parts separate

title: Learn Robotics with Raspberry Pi
tagline: Build a two-wheeled robot and teach it to see and avoid things
summary: Matt Timmons-Brown walks readers through wiring and coding a two-wheeled Raspberry Pi robot in Python 3. The robot gains new abilities chapter by chapter, from remote control to obstacle avoidance, line following and camera-based object recognition.
highlights: One robot that keeps getting smarter makes progress easy to see
Covers practical electronics like power and wiring, along with code
Introduces computer vision with the Pi camera
considerations: Robot parts and a Raspberry Pi are bought separately
Written around older Pi models (3A+/3B+/Zero W recommended), so some steps may need adapting for a Pi 5
requiresDevice: Raspberry Pi and robot parts (not included)

glance.bestFor: want to build and code a Raspberry Pi robot step by step
glance.inTheBox: Book; Raspberry Pi and robot parts sold separately

title: Make: Electronics: Learning by Discovery
tagline: The hands-on electronics primer many makers learned from
summary: Charles Platt teaches electronics through experiments: readers build, test and sometimes deliberately break components to see what happens, then learn the theory behind the result. It progresses from basic circuits to switching, chips and soldered projects.
highlights: Experiment first, explanation second, which helps the ideas stick
Clear photos and diagrams for every step
Deep enough to stay useful well into high school and beyond
considerations: Components and tools are bought separately
Written for adults, so younger teens may want some guidance

glance.bestFor: learn best by experimenting first
glance.inTheBox: Book; components and tools sold separately

title: Arduino Workshop, 2nd Edition
tagline: 65 Arduino projects to try after the starter kit runs out
summary: John Boxall's project book teaches Arduino through 65 builds that combine wiring and code, covering displays, sensors, motors, wireless communication and more. It's a natural next step for a teen who has finished a starter kit and wants new ideas.
highlights: A large number of projects that get steadily harder
Explains the code line by line, so readers can adapt it
Pairs well with an official Arduino or ELEGOO kit
considerations: Needs an Arduino board and parts, bought separately
Needs a computer to program the board

glance.bestFor: have finished a starter kit and want new projects
glance.inTheBox: Book with 65 projects; Arduino and parts sold separately
